questions.q: A wave is a disturbance that travels through a medium from a source to a detector. What does the wave transfer?
options: It transfers particles of the medium along with the disturbance
It transfers energy without any net movement of matter or particles
It transfers both energy and matter equally from source to detector
It transfers the medium itself outwards from the source
questions.explanation: A wave transfers energy without any net movement of particles. When a rock is thrown into a still pond, twigs or lily pads on the surface bob up and down rather than being carried along; it is the energy that travels outwards, not the water itself.

questions.q: In a transverse wave, how does the disturbance caused by the transfer of energy act relative to the direction of the wave?
options: Parallel to the direction of the wave, forming compressions
Perpendicularly to the direction of the wave itself, forming crests and troughs
In a circular path around the direction of the wave
Opposite to the direction the wave is moving
questions.explanation: A transverse wave is one in which the disturbance acts perpendicularly to the direction of the wave itself. The highest points of transverse waves are called crests or peaks, while the lowest points are called troughs. Water ripples and all electromagnetic waves are transverse.

questions.q: A longitudinal wave (also called a compression wave) alternately pushes the particles of the medium together and pulls them apart. What are the regions where the particles are crowded closest together called?
options: Crests
Compressions
Rarefactions
Troughs
questions.explanation: In a longitudinal wave the disturbance moves in the same direction as the wave. The positions where the particles are crowded together closest are called compressions, and those where the particles are spread furthest apart are called rarefactions. Sound waves move as longitudinal waves.

questions.q: What is the key difference between mechanical waves and electromagnetic waves in how they propagate energy from place to place?
options: Mechanical waves travel faster than electromagnetic waves in a vacuum
Mechanical waves transfer energy through the motion of the particles of a medium, while electromagnetic waves do not need a medium to travel in
Electromagnetic waves require a medium of particles, while mechanical waves travel through empty space
Both mechanical and electromagnetic waves transfer particles, not energy
questions.explanation: Mechanical waves involve the transfer of energy through a medium by the motion of the particles of the medium itself, so they cannot travel through a vacuum. Electromagnetic waves are transverse oscillations of electric and magnetic force fields and do not need a medium to travel in.

questions.q: How does the amplitude of a wave relate to the energy associated with the wave?
options: The bigger the amplitude of the wave, the more energy it has
Amplitude has no relationship to the wave's energy
The smaller the amplitude, the more energy the wave carries
Amplitude determines the wave's speed, not its energy
questions.explanation: The amplitude, A, of a wave relates to the amount of energy associated with the wave: the bigger the amplitude, the more energy it has. Amplitude is the maximum displacement of a particle from the normal, undisturbed position of the medium.

questions.q: What is the speed of a sound wave if it has a period of 2.0 ms and a wavelength of 68 cm?
questions.explanation: Time must be expressed in seconds and length in metres before substituting. Using the wave equation \(v = f\lambda\) with \(f = 1/T\) gives \(v = \lambda/T = 0.68 / (2.0\times10^{-3}) = 340\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), the speed of sound in air.

questions.q: A displacement-position graph (a snapshot of a slinky spring) shows a wavelength of 1.6 m. Waves were sent through the slinky at a rate of 2 per second. Use the wave equation to determine the speed of the wave.
questions.explanation: A displacement-position graph is a 'snapshot' of the wave at one instant, from which the wavelength (distance between successive peaks) is read as 1.6 m. With the frequency given as 2 per second, the wave equation gives \(v = f\lambda = 2 \times 1.6 = 3.2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

questions.q: From memory: define the period, frequency and wavelength of a periodic wave, and state how the period and frequency are related.
keyPoints: The period (T) is the time taken for a source to produce one complete wave, measured in seconds.
The frequency (f) is the number of waves that pass a location in one second, measured in hertz (Hz), where 1 Hz = 1 s⁻¹.
The wavelength (λ) is the distance between successive waves, e.g. crest to crest, measured in metres.
Frequency is the reciprocal of period: T = 1/f.
questions.explanation: If you recalled all three definitions with their units and stated that frequency equals the reciprocal of the period (T = 1/f), grade yourself Good or Easy. For example, middle C at 256 Hz has a period of 1/256 = 3.9 ms.

questions.q: In your own words: explain the difference between the wave speed and the particle speed, using an ocean wave as an example.
keyPoints: The wave speed is how fast the disturbance or pattern travels through the medium — the v in the wave equation v = fλ.
The particle speed is how fast an individual particle of the medium oscillates back and forth about its rest position.
These are completely different and unrelated: on the ocean the wave may race along at several metres per second while any given water molecule just bobs up and down slowly in place.
questions.explanation: The trap is thinking the medium travels with the wave; it doesn't. The wave equation gives the speed of the energy through the medium, not the speed of the particles. If you separated the two clearly, grade Good or Easy.

questions.q: All electromagnetic waves — radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray and gamma — travel through a vacuum at the same speed. How do they differ from one another?
options: They travel at different speeds depending on their frequency
They differ only in frequency and wavelength, linked by the wave equation v = fλ
They differ in speed because higher-frequency waves carry more energy
They differ in the medium each one requires to travel
questions.explanation: Every electromagnetic wave travels at the speed of light, about 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ in a vacuum, because speed depends on the medium (here empty space), not on the frequency. A radio wave and a gamma ray are the same kind of thing travelling at the same speed, differing only in frequency and wavelength, stitched together by v = fλ.
